title: Reservations about Fletcher Henderson's recordings
summary: Briggs found the Henderson arrangements and tenor tone rough and wanted more refinement for patrons, though he admired Buster Bailey.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: And I'd say Fletcher Anderson, his arrangements were good, but to my liking, I think they were a little -- that's the way I feel.
You mean the arrangements or the way they were played?
They were played. Maybe I'd say arrangments, maybe the way they were played.
Maybe a little too much -- bad recording or I don't know, 'cause when you hear a saxophone tenor, his tone was just -- waivers like a billy goat.
That's not so good. I'm not criticizing, I'm just saying what I've heard, you see.

And the way I feel, and the way I think that the patrons would accept or won't accept, you see. That's why I figured, I know that Fletcher Henderson had wonderful men with him, I know them practically all, but it's just one of those things that what can you do -- I'm not criticizing, I'm just saying what I would prefer, -- I would prefer more, a little more culture, you see.
Exactly. And in the sense that I'm playing for patrons, you see.
That I think the patrons would appreciate, maybe have appreciated more, if the tones of the instruments and everything were more embellished.

And I am sure, that they could have been much better, because they had men like Buster Bailey, and Buster was a great man, great musician, great -- very great clarinet player and musician. And it was just one of those things, I guess, but I don't know.
Well, those guys drank -- did an awful lot of drinking in that band too, that may have been part of it.
